title: Research Bite #20: Three Options Are Optimal for Multiple-Choice Items
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #20 covers Michael C. Rodriguez's meta-analysis "Three Options Are Optimal for Multiple-Choice Items," which synthesizes 80 years of research on how the number of answer options in multiple-choice questions affects item difficulty, discrimination, reliability, and validity. Rodriguez's pooled results point consistently to three options -- one correct answer plus two well-constructed distractors -- as the sweet spot, with additional options adding little psychometric value while costing item-writing time. Because shorter items take less time to answer, three-option formats let teachers fit more questions into the same testing window, which in turn improves content coverage and overall test reliability. The analysis also flags a specific trap: removing distractors at random to shorten a test is measurably worse for reliability than removing the distractors that data show are ineffective, so any trimming has to be done deliberately rather than casually. Barton's classroom takeaway is that item-writing guidelines calling for four or five options should be revised, and that teachers' energy is better spent crafting two genuinely plausible distractors than padding out extra, implausible ones.
points: The headline finding -- three options (one correct, two distractors) match or beat four- and five-option items on psychometric quality -- directly overturns the common item-writing convention of requiring four options.
Fewer, better-targeted distractors free up testing time that can be reinvested in more items per test, improving content coverage and reliability.

The distinction between random distractor removal (harmful to reliability) and removal based on which distractors are actually ineffective (safe) is a practical trap for anyone shortening an existing test.
The paper's reframing of the real lever as distractor quality, not distractor quantity -- a plausible distractor does the work that several implausible ones can't.
quotes: This meta-analysis synthesizes 80 years of research on multiple-choice item writing, focusing on the optimal number of response options.
Results indicate that three options are generally optimal, maximizing test efficiency and potentially improving content coverage.
However, the method of distractor removal significantly impacts reliability, with random removal proving detrimental.
Teachers can save time by creating only two plausible distractors instead of three or four, without compromising the quality of the test.

Instead of focusing on creating more distractors, teachers should focus on creating high-quality, plausible distractors. The quality of the distractors, not the number of them, is what guards against awarding undeserved credit.

When reducing the number of options, randomly deleting distractors can be more detrimental to reliability than deleting ineffective distractors. Teachers should consider which distractors to eliminate thoughtfully.
